confidence_note: The airport scenario (two travelers, 30 minutes vs 5 minutes late) is Kahneman and Tversky's simulation-heuristic example from their 1982 chapter; web sources confirm Lewis's book covers the simulation heuristic and the idea of 'undoing' but I did not read Lewis's own page. The travelers' names (Mr. Crane, Mr. Tees) and the 96 percent figure come from the 1982 chapter, not verified in Lewis's text; the 96 percent is used only as 'nearly all' of the people asked. Omitted: any dates, Kahneman's personal reactions, page-level wording. The reference text's claim that the man who misses by five minutes relives an alternative story 'again and again' is not verified and is not used.
facts: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied how the mind imagines how things could have turned out differently; they called this the simulation heuristic, linked to what Kahneman called the rule of undoing.
Their example: two travelers, Mr. Crane and Mr. Tees, ride to the airport in the same limousine, stuck in the same traffic jam.
Both arrive 30 minutes after their flights were scheduled to leave.
Mr. Crane is told his flight left on time. Mr. Tees is told his flight was delayed and left only five minutes ago.
Asked which man is more upset, nearly all the people asked (96 percent in the 1982 chapter) said Mr. Tees.
Both men missed their planes by the same facts; the difference lies only in how easy it is to imagine catching it, so the five-minute man can picture himself making it.
Lewis presents this as part of the pair's work showing that the mind judges outcomes against imagined alternatives, not only against what happened.
scene_details: the same limousine and the same traffic jam
thirty minutes late versus five minutes late
a flight that left five minutes ago
tension: Two men miss the same kind of flight for the same reason, yet nearly everyone says one will hurt more.
opening_idea: Start in the limousine: same traffic, same airport, two missed flights, and a gap of 25 minutes that changes everything.

lessons.idea: Regret is measured against the alternative you can easily imagine, so near misses sting more than clear misses, even when the loss is the same.
lessons.anchor: Mr. Tees, told his flight left five minutes ago

reflect_final: Think of a recent disappointment that hurt more than it should have: which easy-to-imagine 'if only' was making it worse, and is it a fact or just a picture?

use_cases.situation: A friend keeps replaying a narrow loss, like a missed deadline by an hour.
use_cases.move: Say that Mr. Tees missed his flight just like Mr. Crane; the extra pain came from how close the other ending looked. Ask what actually changed besides the picture.

use_cases.situation: After a project almost succeeded, your team is sour.
use_cases.move: Name the near miss aloud and ask which 'if only' is a fact you can use next time and which is only a picture.

use_cases.situation: You are replaying a decision at night.
use_cases.move: Write down the one 'if only' that keeps returning and ask whether anyone could have known it then.

pocket_idea: Mr. Tees lost the same flight as Mr. Crane; only the picture of catching it was closer.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Two men miss the same flight and nearly everyone says the one who was five minutes late hurts more.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Kahneman and Tversky: two travelers stuck in the same traffic, both late by thirty minutes; one told his flight left on time, the other that it left five minutes ago. Nearly everyone says the second suffers more. Same loss, closer alternative.
